turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What can I do for you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the knee, doctor. I'm worried sick about it, I really am.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which knee?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh the rain was pouring and the bus was jammed, I was ages getting across, and then—
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which knee?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The right. Sorry. Um, going down the stairs it catches me, and at night it's wicked.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months... no, nearer five months. It came on after the new year.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I end up like my mother? She had the two knees done. I'm not able for an operation, I just—
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop there. Morning stiffness?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, about ten minutes till I get going. Is that bad? Should I be worried if it's only—
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Locking? Giving way?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It doesn't lock, and it hasn't given way.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hips or back?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just the right knee. Nothing else.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Could it be a clot though? I was reading last night and I haven't slept... well, I do sleep, but then I'm googling like a mad thing.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a clot. Stairs and night pain is the joint. What are you putting on it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac gel from the chemist. I rub it on twice a day. One percent, I think... maybe. I never properly looked at the tube.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tablets?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother takes metformin for his sugar, the diabetes, and he says tablets wrecked his stomach, so I got nervous, but—
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your tablets.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac, the tablets, from the chemist as well. Only sometimes, when the pain is bad. Not every day.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Strength?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams... no, seventy-five. The box says seventy-five. One of them, maybe two or three times in the week.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach problems?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No stomach problems. None.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yes. A small bit of heartburn if I take the tablet late in the evening. I couldn't tell you when that started. I didn't think it counted.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that dangerous? Do I stop the tablets altogether? The gel is the same drug, isn't it, will that burn me too? I've been fretting all week.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gel is grand. If the heartburn comes, leave the tablets off. If you take one, take it with food, not on an empty stomach.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Eleven stone... no, sorry, twelve stone four. I always mix it up. They weighed me in the surgery last month.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): That weight is loading the knee. Cut the biscuits. Short walks.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister is on biotin, big tablets, for her hair. Would that do the knee any good? She keeps telling me to try it. Is it safe with the diclofenac? How many would I even take?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. That's your sister's. Biotin will not fix the knee. Don't start it.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair enough. God, the weather though. I was telling my granddaughter, she's seven, she had camogie on Saturday and the rain never stopped. They were out on the pitch the whole hour. She thought it was brilliant, of course.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): They were soaked, and she lost one sock in the dressing room, just one sock. The cars around the school were bumper to bumper. We laughed the whole way home on the bus.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The knee.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. So what will you do? Physio? Someone said an injection. I'm terrified of needles, but if it works I'll do it. Does it work? How sore is it? Can you walk the same day?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Physio is one option. A steroid injection into the knee is another. I am not booking either today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Which is better though? If I try the physio first, can I still have the injection if it's no good? And how long are people waiting? The lists are a fright, aren't they?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either can wait. We decide next time, if the pain is still there.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it arthritis? Please say it straight. I've had myself in a wheelchair by Christmas, which is ridiculous, I know, but at three in the morning it doesn't feel ridiculous.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most likely osteoarthritis of the right knee. I can't confirm that without an x-ray, and I am not ordering one today.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No x-ray? Is that safe? What if it's something else, a tumour or that? I know I sound mad.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing suggests a tumour. Osteoarthritis fits. Come back in six weeks.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. And if it gets worse before that, the stairs are a killer, what do I do? Ring you? Go back to the chemist?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ring the surgery if you cannot walk on it or it swells right up. Otherwise the gel twice a day, the tablets only now and again with food, and keep moving.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the heartburn go if I ease off the tablets? And should I be on something for the stomach? I don't want an ulcer. My head is racing.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off and it should settle. No stomach tablet from me today. Six weeks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. I'll try to stay off Google. Thanks a million.
